title: Five Workers, a Grandmother's Plot and a Three-Kilo Pair of Shoes
dek: In 2004 Bethlehem Tilahun Alemu opened a shoe workshop in the Addis Ababa neighbourhood where she grew up, paid for it herself and learned the craft as she went.

story.event: Starting a tyre-soled shoe workshop with five workers on her grandmother's land in Zenabwork
story.summary: In 2004 Bethlehem Tilahun Alemu, an accountant by training, started soleRebels with five workers in a workshop on her grandmother's plot in Zenabwork, Addis Ababa, making shoes based on the tyre-soled selate sandal. She financed it herself, by her account with less than 5,000 US dollars, and has said the first pair weighed three kilos. The company became a World Fair Trade Organization-certified brand selling abroad and stayed family-owned.
paragraphs: In 2004 Bethlehem Tilahun Alemu set up a workshop on a plot of land that belonged to her grandmother in Zenabwork, one of the poorest neighbourhoods of Addis Ababa and the one she had grown up in. Her grandmother had been among its first settlers, a migrant from Gojjam. Alemu, born in 1980, had studied accountancy at Unity University and worked for leather and clothing firms. Now, as she later put it, there were five workers and herself. She called the company soleRebels.

What she knew best was the neighbourhood. She had watched relatives spin cotton by hand and weavers work wooden looms, and she saw skilled neighbours and family members shut out of even simple jobs by poverty and stigma. All around her people wore the selate, a sandal soled with old tyres that Ethiopian fighters had made common during the Italian occupation. She had also heard a great deal about poverty alleviation and decided the bar was set too low; she wanted a brand good enough to sell anywhere. She paid for it herself. Speaking in Addis Ababa in 2013, she put the start-up money at under 5,000 US dollars, and said that a business sponsored by a donor means "you carry that flag with you, and it doesn't feel good."

The early work was humbling. "We didn't know how to make shoes," she told that audience. The first pair they made weighed three kilos, and she could not walk in them. At her first exhibition in the city, passers-by laughed at shoes made from scrap. Getting online from Addis was hard, she later told SBS News, yet she sold abroad from the start, first through platforms such as Amazon, and sent samples all over the world. Skilled makers were hired, the designs improved, and one of the early orders, she said, was for 5,000 pairs.

By 2012 soleRebels was certified by the World Fair Trade Organization and selling in more than 50 countries, and she was still running it from Zenabwork. By 2015, ILO News reported, it employed more than 100 local workers at three to five times the industry's usual pay. In 2014 she said it was wholly family-owned and had never taken outside investment.

quote.text: For no limit can be set to skill, neither is there any craftsman that possesseth full advantages.
quote.work: The Instruction of Ptahhotep (and of Ke'gemni)
quote.source_title: The Instruction of Ptah-Hotep and the Instruction of Ke'Gemni, tr. Battiscombe G. Gunn, Project Gutenberg eBook #30508
quote.connection: Alemu's workshop began with an aim far ahead of its skill. Ptahhotep, an old vizier instructing his son, says that skill has no fixed ceiling and no craftsman ever starts with every advantage. Read beside him, the unwearable first pair is the opening of a craft rather than a judgement on the idea.

reflection: There is something steadying about a first pair of shoes that nobody could walk in. Alemu had a clear aim and very little of the craft, and she did not wait to master the craft before starting. The heavy pair was not a verdict on the idea; it was the first lesson in a skill that, as Ptahhotep says, never reaches its limit.

You will have mornings when something you have made looks clumsy beside what you pictured: a page of notes, a plan, a conversation you handled badly. Clumsy and early are not the same as wrong. Most good work has an unwearable first version somewhere behind it.
invitation: Look at one early piece of your own work that embarrasses you a little. Write down one thing it taught you, then leave it as it is today, without fixing it.

research_notes: Founding year: the slate said 2005, and SBS News (2019) says she founded it in 2005 and quotes her saying she started '14 years ago'. Her interviews with Knowledge at Wharton (2012) and ILO News (2015) both give 2004, AWiB (2013) says 'nine years ago' and The Long + Short (2014) 'a decade on', so the story uses 2004. The first five people: Wharton and ILO say 'five workers', The Long + Short 'five artisans', AWiB 'five embroiderers', and SBS 'her brothers and neighbours'; the story says only 'five workers'. Spelling of the neighbourhood varies (Zenabwork, Zenabework, Zenebework); the story follows ILO and The Long + Short. Workforce figures differ: Wharton (2012) says 'hundreds of workers', AWiB (2013) reports 120, ILO (2015) more than 100 local workers, SBS (2019) 300; the story uses ILO's conservative 'more than 100 local workers' and attributes it. Store counts also differ (The Long + Short gives both 10 and 11 in 2014; ILO gives 18 in 2015), so the story gives none. Revenue is not used: The Long + Short notes that she tends to speak of projected rather than actual turnover. The start-up sum (under USD 5,000), the three-kilo first pair, the laughter at her first exhibition and the 5,000-pair early order rest on AWiB's report of her own talk in Addis Ababa on 7 March 2013 and are attributed to her; one secondary brand-profile site (Brandmine, not cited) says the first prototypes weighed six kilograms, so the story keeps her figure as AWiB reported it. The ILO's 2019 '100 Years – 100 Lives' article repeats the 2015 ILO News text almost word for word, so the 2015 original is cited. The Ptahhotep line is the second half of precept 1, which opens with the better-known 'Be not proud because thou art learned'; the excerpt begins at a sentence start.
